source: a16z Podcast — AI demand outrunning compute supply; frontier-lab revenue is self-determined, reinvestment math, not necessarily winner-take-all
summary: Hyperscalers should be valued on EV/net PP&E as an AI-era price-to-book analog, with some showing obvious inefficiencies
summary_extended: Baker argues that the correct valuation framework for hyperscalers in the AI era is EV divided by net PP&E, treating net PP&E as a proxy for compute capacity — effectively an AI-era price-to-book ratio where the market is pricing what it believes each company will monetize from its compute fleet. He states he 'increasingly' uses this lens, suggesting it is a recent and deliberate analytical shift rather than a passing observation. Critically, Baker flags 'pretty obvious inefficiencies' across the hyperscaler group on this metric, implying that some names are materially mispriced relative to others on a compute-value basis. The investment implication is a relative-value trade within the hyperscaler cohort — buying the names with lower EV/net PP&E (underpriced compute) and potentially underweighting those with higher multiples — though Baker does not name specific winners or losers. No specific numbers or target multiples are cited, but the framework is actionable as a screening tool across the major cloud/AI infrastructure operators.
detail: Baker says he increasingly looks at hyperscalers on EV to net PP&E because net PP&E is compute, and the market is effectively pricing what it thinks they'll monetize their compute fleet at. He notes 'some pretty obvious inefficiencies' in this metric across the group — implying relative value opportunities.
confidence_evidence: Baker describes this as his current analytical framework ('I increasingly look at') and flags 'pretty obvious inefficiencies' without naming specific names

ticker_audit.reasoning: Microsoft is one of the core hyperscalers (Azure) with substantial net PP&E from AI datacenter buildout; the EV/net PP&E framework directly applies to it as a valuation subject.
Alphabet/Google Cloud is a primary hyperscaler with massive compute PP&E; the thesis directly applies as a valuation framework for this company.
Amazon Web Services is the largest cloud provider with the most significant net PP&E among hyperscalers; the EV/net PP&E framework is directly applicable.

Meta is not a hyperscaler in the cloud-services sense — it does not sell compute to third parties. While it has large PP&E from AI infrastructure, Baker's framework is about monetizing compute fleets via cloud/AI services, which is not Meta's model. Meta is likely bleed-over from adjacent AI capex discussion.
